claim: Phantom perceptions like tinnitus occur without any identifiable environmental or bodily source.
source_text: Phantom perceptions like tinnitus occur without any identifiable environmental or bodily source.
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional statement about tinnitus that draws from established scientific understanding of the condition.

claim: Approximately 10–15% of the young to middle-aged adult population experience tinnitus.
source_text: Approximately 10–15% of the young to middle-aged adult population experience tinnitus as a common auditory phantom perception, with greater prevalence of 24% in older adults
evidence_reasoning: This prevalence statistic is supported by citations to Biswas et al., 2022; Henry et al., 2020; Jarach et al., 2022.

claim: The prevalence of tinnitus is 24% in older adults.
source_text: Approximately 10–15% of the young to middle-aged adult population experience tinnitus as a common auditory phantom perception, with greater prevalence of 24% in older adults
evidence_reasoning: This prevalence statistic is supported by citations to Biswas et al., 2022; Henry et al., 2020; Jarach et al., 2022.

claim: Bothersome tinnitus poses a significant detriment to quality of life due to reduced sleep quality, substantially increased distress, and anxiety.
source_text: For a smaller portion of the population, the sensation of bothersome tinnitus poses a significant detriment to quality of life, due to reduced sleep quality, substantially increased distress, and anxiety
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citation to Dobie, 2003.

claim: The impact of tinnitus on quality of life is largely independent of the intensity or duration of the phantom perception.
source_text: all largely independent of the intensity or duration of the phantom perception
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Kandeepan et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2014.

claim: Hearing loss has been identified as a main risk factor for tinnitus.
source_text: Hearing loss has been identified as a main risk factor for tinnitus
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: For 75–80% of people with tinnitus, objective audiometric testing indicates hearing loss.
source_text: Indeed, for 75–80% of people with tinnitus, objective audiometric testing indicates hearing loss
evidence_reasoning: This statistic is supported by citation to Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2017.

claim: Some form of auditory damage facilitates tinnitus development even without clear audiometric changes.
source_text: Previous findings support the idea that some form of auditory damage – even without clear audiometric changes – facilitates tinnitus development
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2006; Schaette and McAlpine, 2011; Schaette et al., 2012; Weisz et al., 2006.

claim: Increased neural activity following hearing loss has been observed in animal models.
source_text: Based on the observation of increased neural activity following hearing loss in animal models
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Eggermont and Roberts, 2004; Roberts et al., 2010.

claim: Reduced auditory input following hearing damage leads neurons in the auditory pathway to increase their responsivity to restore their mean activity level.
source_text: a still-influential 'altered-gain' view holds that reduced auditory input following hearing damage leads neurons in the auditory pathway to increase their responsivity, thereby restoring their mean activity level
evidence_reasoning: This theoretical framework is supported by citations to Schaette and Kempter, 2006; Sedley, 2019a.

claim: Empirical support for tinnitus frameworks in humans is weak, difficult to replicate, and marked by strong interindividual variability.
source_text: However, apart from a significant shortage of data bridging animal and human research in these different frameworks, empirical support in humans is weak, difficult to replicate, and marked by strong interindividual variability
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Eggermont and Roberts, 2015; Elgoyhen et al., 2015; Reisinger et al., 2023.

claim: People with hearing loss do not necessarily experience tinnitus.
source_text: (1) People with hearing loss do not necessarily experience tinnitus
evidence_reasoning: This explanatory challenge is supported by citation to Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2017.

claim: The onsets of tinnitus and hearing loss often do not occur at the same time.
source_text: (2) The onsets of tinnitus and hearing loss often do not occur at the same time
evidence_reasoning: This explanatory challenge is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2010.

claim: Not all cases of acute tinnitus transform into chronic tinnitus.
source_text: (3) Not all cases of acute tinnitus transform into chronic tinnitus
evidence_reasoning: This explanatory challenge is supported by citations to Mühlmeier et al., 2016; Vielsmeier et al., 2020.

claim: Spontaneous activity in the auditory pathway acts as a precursor of tinnitus.
source_text: The framework holds that spontaneous activity in the auditory pathway acts as a precursor of tinnitus.
evidence_reasoning: This is part of the Bayesian inference framework for tinnitus perception referenced to Sedley et al., 2016a.

claim: In the healthy auditory system, spontaneous activity is 'ignored' due to the default prior of silence.
source_text: In the healthy auditory system, spontaneous activity is 'ignored', due to the default prior of silence.
evidence_reasoning: This is part of the Bayesian inference framework and is inferred from the theoretical model presented in the cited work.

claim: Certain circumstances can shift the prior expectation such that a particular sound is expected.
source_text: However, certain circumstances can shift this prior, such that a particular sound is expected
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Hullfish et al., 2019; Sedley et al., 2016b.

claim: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus using EEG evoked responses.
source_text: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus, which is in line with the predictive-coding framework using either EEG evoked responses
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Mohan et al., 2022; Sedley et al., 2019b.

claim: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus using computational modeling.
source_text: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus, which is in line with the predictive-coding framework using either EEG evoked responses (Mohan et al., 2022; Sedley et al., 2019b) or computational modeling
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2021.

claim: Individuals with stronger predictive tendencies are more vulnerable to developing tinnitus.
source_text: In this work we hypothesized that, given that forming a strong sensory prediction based on weak sensory evidence is thought to be a key process in developing tinnitus, individuals with stronger predictive tendencies are more vulnerable to developing tinnitus
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' hypothesis for their study, representing speculative reasoning about tinnitus vulnerability.

claim: A recently established experimental approach shows anticipatory activations of tonotopically specific auditory templates for regular tone sequences.
source_text: We utilized a powerful, recently established experimental approach (Demarchi et al., 2019) showing anticipatory activations of tonotopically specific auditory templates for regular tone sequences.
evidence_reasoning: This claim about the experimental approach is supported by citation to Demarchi et al., 2019.

claim: In Study 1, 34 individuals with tinnitus participated in the experiment.
source_text: In Study 1, a total of 34 individuals with tinnitus (17 females, age 20–67 years, mean = 45.12, sd = 13.65) participated in the experiment.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of the study's participant data.

claim: In Study 1, 25 individuals with tinnitus were age-matched with the control group and used for group comparisons.
source_text: Within this group, 25 individuals (16 females, age 20–66 years, mean = 40.92, sd = 13.17) were age-matched (in all cases but one both age- and sex-matched) with the control group and used for group comparisons.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of the study's participant matching procedure.

claim: In Study 1, standardized pure-tone audiometric testing was performed in 31 out of 34 tinnitus participants.
source_text: Standardized pure-tone audiometric testing for frequencies from 125 Hz to 8 kHz was performed in 31 out of 34 tinnitus participants using Interacoustic AS608 audiometer.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of the audiometric testing performed in the study.

claim: In Study 1, 25 individuals reporting no relevant audiological, neurological or psychiatric treatment history took part as a control group.
source_text: 25 individuals (16 females, age 21–65 years, mean = 41.56, sd = 13.68) reporting no relevant audiological, neurological or psychiatric treatment history took part as a control group.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of the control group characteristics.

claim: In Study 1, no differences in age were shown between the tinnitus and control samples.
source_text: No differences were shown for age between the samples (t = 0.17, p = 0.89).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the study comparing age between groups.

claim: In Study 1, pure-tone audiometric testing was not included for the control subjects, making group comparisons between hearing thresholds not feasible.
source_text: As pure-tone audiometric testing was not included for the control subjects, group comparisons between hearing thresholds were not feasible.

claim: In Study 2, 40 individuals with tinnitus and 40 hearing-, age-, and sex-matched control subjects completed the experiment.
source_text: In Study 2, 40 individuals with tinnitus (16 females, age 24–74 years, mean = 57.73, sd = 14.12), as well as 40 hearing-, age-, and sex-matched control subjects (16 females, age 24–76 years, mean = 57.43, sd = 13.94) completed the experiment.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of the study's participant data.

claim: In Study 2, inclusion criteria for the tinnitus group were a tinnitus duration of more than 6 months.
source_text: For the tinnitus group, inclusion criteria were a tinnitus duration of more than 6 months.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct statement of the study's inclusion criteria.

claim: In Study 2, no participants with psychiatric or neurological diseases were included in the sample.
source_text: No participants with psychiatric or neurological diseases were included in the sample.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct statement of the study's exclusion criteria.

claim: In Study 2, hearing loss was defined by a hearing threshold higher than 30 dB HL in at least one frequency.
source_text: We also performed pure-tone audiometric testing and defined hearing loss by a hearing threshold higher than 30 dB HL in at least one frequency.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct statement of the operational definition used in the study.

claim: In Study 2, four individuals with tinnitus did not show any audiometric abnormality.
source_text: Four individuals with tinnitus did not show any audiometric abnormality
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of audiometric findings in the study.

claim: In Study 2, no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups were found for the left ear.
source_text: Using independent t-tests, we found no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups for the left (t = −1.19, p = 0.238) and right ear (t = −1.72, p = 0.09).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the study comparing hearing status between groups.

claim: In Study 2, no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups were found for the right ear.
source_text: Using independent t-tests, we found no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups for the left (t = −1.19, p = 0.238) and right ear (t = −1.72, p = 0.09).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the study comparing hearing status between groups.

claim: In Study 1, four different pure tones were presented with carrier frequencies logarithmically spaced between 200 and 2000 Hz.
source_text: In Study 1, four different pure (sinusoidal) tones were presented, with carrier frequencies logarithmically spaced between 200 and 2000 Hz (200, 431, 928, and 2000 Hz)
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli used.

claim: In Study 2, carrier frequencies of the four tones were logarithmically spaced between approximately 440 and 1043 Hz.
source_text: In Study 2, carrier frequencies of the four tones were logarithmically spaced between approximately 440 and 1043 Hz (i.e. 440, 587, 782, and 1043 Hz).
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli used.

claim: In both Study 1 and Study 2, each tone lasted 100 ms and was tapered at both ends with 5 ms linearly ascending/descending periods.
source_text: In both designs, each tone lasted 100 ms, tapered at both ends with 5 ms linearly ascending/descending periods
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the stimulus characteristics.

claim: In both Study 1 and Study 2, sounds were presented at a constant 3-Hz stimulation rate.
source_text: and we presented the sounds at a constant 3-Hz stimulation rate.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the stimulus presentation rate.

claim: In Study 1, four blocks of tone sequences comprising 4000 stimuli were presented, each lasting approximately 22 min.
source_text: In Study 1, we presented four blocks of tone sequences comprising 4000 stimuli, each lasting approximately 22 min.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: In Study 1, four entropy conditions were used for the design: random, midminus, midplus, and ordered.
source_text: We used four entropy conditions for the design. The random condition had the highest entropy (i.e. the lowest regularity), and the transition probabilities from one sound to another were equal, preventing any possibility of accurately predicting upcoming stimuli. In contrast, the ordered condition had the lowest entropy level (i.e. the highest regularity), and in 75% of trials, one sound was followed by a specific other sound. In 25% of trials, the same sound was repeated. Additionally, two intermediate entropy conditions were included, labeled here as midminus and midplus.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental conditions.

claim: In Study 1, a randomly chosen 10% of the sounds were omitted in all conditions.
source_text: Furthermore, a randomly chosen 10% of the sounds were omitted in all conditions (not included in the current analysis), resulting in 900 sound trials and 100 omission trials per entropy block, that is 3600 sounds and 400 omissions in total.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: In Study 2, fewer stimuli were used and sound sequences were combined into two continuous blocks, each lasting approximately 8 min.
source_text: In Study 2, fewer stimuli were used, and we combined the sound sequences solely into two continuous blocks, each lasting approximately 8 min.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: In Study 2, no omissions were included and participants solely listened to sounds that were either random or ordered.
source_text: Furthermore, no omissions were included, and participants solely listened to sounds that were either random or ordered.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: Magnetic brain activity was measured using a whole-head MEG with 102 magnetometers and 204 orthogonally placed planar gradiometers.
source_text: We measured magnetic brain activity using a whole-head MEG (Triux, MEGIN Oy, Finland), in which brain signals were captured by 102 magnetometers and 204 orthogonally placed planar gradiometers.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the measurement equipment used.

claim: MEG data was sampled at a rate of 1000 Hz.
source_text: Participants sat in a dimly lit magnetically shielded room (AK3b, Vacuumschmelze, Germany) and were measured with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the data acquisition parameters.

claim: A signal-space separation algorithm was used to reduce external noise from the MEG signal.
source_text: We used a signal-space separation algorithm (SSS Taulu and Kajola, 2005) implemented in the Maxfilter program (version 2.2.15) to reduce external noise from the MEG signal
evidence_reasoning: This describes the preprocessing method used, supported by citation to Taulu and Kajola, 2005.

claim: The analyses were based on magnetometers only, since information between magnetometers and gradiometers is mixed after the Maxfilter step.
source_text: The analyses were based on magnetometers only, since information between magnetometers and gradiometers is mixed after the Maxfilter step
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological decision supported by citation to Garcés et al., 2017.

claim: In Study 1, an average of 3.6 ICA components were removed.
source_text: In Study 1, an average of 3.6 components (sd = 1.2) were removed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct report of the preprocessing steps applied to the data.

source_text: In Study 2, an average of 2.3 components (sd = 0.72) were removed in the tinnitus group

claim: A multiclass linear discriminant analysis classifier was trained on each sample point of the random condition.
source_text: We trained a multiclass linear discriminant analysis classifier on each sample point of the random condition
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct description of the analysis method used.

claim: A temporal generalization method was used to analyze the ability of the classifier to generalize across time points.
source_text: Additionally, we used a temporal generalization method (King and Dehaene, 2014) to analyze the ability of the classifier to generalize across time points in the training set to time points in the testing set.

claim: In Study 1, both groups exhibited a rapid increase of decoding accuracy following sound onset, robustly observed at an individual level.
source_text: Both groups exhibited a rapid increase of decoding accuracy following sound onset, robustly observed at an individual level

source_text: Interestingly, accuracy transiently increased approximately 100 ms after the subsequent stimulus onset (i.e. 450–500 ms after the to-be-decoded sound).

claim: In Study 1, no differences in decoding accuracy were found between the tinnitus group and the control group for the random condition.
source_text: Importantly, we found no differences between the tinnitus group and the control group.

claim: In Study 1, bias scores did not differ between the tinnitus and control groups.
source_text: Also, for the same investigation time period, bias scores did not differ between the group (all cluster p's > 0.83, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: In Study 1, individuals with tinnitus encode and reactivate carrier frequencies equally well to individuals without tinnitus when the context is unpredictable.
source_text: Therefore, at a basic level, individuals with tinnitus encode and reactivate carrier frequencies equally well to individuals without tinnitus when the context is unpredictable.

claim: In Study 1, a positive cluster was identified prior to the onset of the to-be-decoded event at approximately –530 to –200 ms.

evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the study showing a significant cluster.

claim: In Study 1, a negative cluster was observed between 360 and 800 ms.

claim: In Study 1, individuals with tinnitus appeared to quickly deactivate carrier-frequency patterns the more regular the sound sequence became.
source_text: caused by inverse tendencies for the tinnitus and control groups (Figure 3A): that is, whereas individuals with tinnitus appeared to quickly deactivate carrier-frequency patterns the more regular the sound sequence became

claim: In Study 1, no significant correlation was found between pre-stimulus β-regression values and hearing thresholds in the tinnitus sample.

claim: In Study 1, Bayes factors for the pre-stimulus correlations provided moderate to strong evidence for the null hypothesis.
source_text: All Bayes factors were found to be between 1/3 and 1/10, that is, providing moderate to strong evidence for the null hypothesis.

claim: In Study 1, no significant correlation was found between post-stimulus β-regression values and hearing thresholds in the tinnitus sample.
source_text: The same tendency was found for the post-stimulus negative cluster for hearing thresholds (rho = −0.13, p = 0.45)

claim: In Study 1, no significant correlation was found between post-stimulus β-regression values and tinnitus loudness in the tinnitus sample.
source_text: The same tendency was found for the post-stimulus negative cluster for hearing thresholds (rho = −0.13, p = 0.45), tinnitus loudness (rho = −0.01, p = 0.95)

claim: In Study 1, no significant correlation was found between post-stimulus β-regression values and tinnitus distress in the tinnitus sample.

evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claim: In Study 1, the lack of relationships between prediction related neural effects with hearing thresholds supports the claim that the effects are strictly regularity-dependent and not driven by low-level auditory processing.
source_text: The lack of relationships between prediction related neural effects with hearing thresholds add further support to the claim that the effects visible in group analysis are strictly regularity-dependent and not driven by low-level auditory processing.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between neural effects and hearing thresholds.

claim: In Study 1, basic processing of carrier frequencies are not altered in tinnitus.
source_text: Our main findings are: (1) basic processing of carrier frequencies are not altered in tinnitus
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the main finding from Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, with increasing regularity of the sequence, individuals with tinnitus show relatively enhanced predictions of frequency information.
source_text: (2) with increasing regularity of the sequence, individuals with tinnitus show relatively enhanced predictions of frequency information

claim: In Study 1, the effect of enhanced predictions in tinnitus is not related to hearing thresholds and tinnitus distress or loudness.
source_text: (3) the effect is not related to hearing thresholds and tinnitus distress or loudness in this sample.

claim: Study 2 was recommended as a registered report by the Peer Community In Registered Reports.
source_text: As mentioned before, Study 2 was by itself already recommended as a registered report by the Peer Community In Registered Reports (https://osf.io/8bv29, Chambers, 2024).

claim: In Study 2, the classifier reliably decoded carrier-frequency information from MEG data for the entire sample.
source_text: As illustrated in Figure 4A (red line), this is clearly the case for the entire sample (t260 = 8.40, 95% CI [0.0092, 0.0148], p < 0.001)

claim: In Study 2, decoding performance peaked at approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset.
source_text: with a rapid increase of decoding performance peaking at ~100 ms

claim: In Study 2, above chance decoding performance lasted throughout the entire post-stimulus period.
source_text: and a slow decrease however with above chance decoding performance lasting throughout the entire post-stimulus period, including a small increase following the subsequent tone presented at 333 ms.

claim: In Study 2, source analyses demonstrated strong activations in the temporal areas in both hemispheres.
source_text: Consecutive source analyses demonstrated strong activations in the temporal areas in both hemispheres for the first time window which were still present in the later time window – however less pronounced and more lateralized

claim: Decoding accuracies in Study 2 were significantly lower than in Study 1.
source_text: However, when comparing the outcomes of both studies, some differences can be noticed. First, a ~30 ms delay can be seen in Study 2 and more importantly, accuracies were significantly lower (t260 = 2.16, 95% CI [0.0005, 0.0109], p = 0.031).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical comparison between the two studies.

claim: The lower decoding accuracies in Study 2 are most likely due to the much narrower sound frequency range compared to Study 1.
source_text: These differences are most likely due modifications of the paradigm, and particularly the much narrower sound frequency range in Study 2 (1.3 octaves) as compared to Study 1 (3.3 octaves), making the decoding more challenging.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the cause of the observed difference in decoding accuracy.

claim: In Study 2, a significant positive cluster was revealed in the pre-stimulus interval when comparing ordered versus random sound conditions.
source_text: When testing on the pre-stimulus interval between –400 and 0 ms, one-sided cluster-based permutation t-tests revealed a significant positive cluster (tsum = 26.2, p = 0.046).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the cluster-based permutation test.

claim: In Study 2, the positive cluster indicated relatively higher decoding accuracies in the tinnitus group, replicating the central finding in Study 1.
source_text: In line with our prediction, this indicated relatively higher decoding accuracies in the tinnitus group and therefore replicated the central finding in Study 1
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of the statistical result in the context of replication.

claim: In Study 2, the effect was most pronounced in the time window between –410 and –310 ms.
source_text: The effect appeared to be most pronounced in the time window between –410 and –310 ms.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from the time-resolved analysis.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores in the tinnitus group did not significantly vary from zero.
source_text: Comparing the prediction scores against zero within each group indicated non-significance for the tinnitus group with t78 = 0.063, 95% CI [–0.0017, 0.0018], p = 0.950.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the one-sample t-test.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores in the control group significantly varied from zero.
source_text: In the group without tinnitus, however, prediction scores significantly varied from zero (t78 = −3.65, 95% CI [–0.0047, –0.0014], p < .001).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the one-sample t-test.

claim: In Study 2, prediction score differences between tinnitus and control groups are driven by below-chance accuracy in the control group at late training time intervals.
source_text: This indeed indicates that prediction score differences between tinnitus and control groups are driven by below-chance accuracy in the control group at these late training time intervals.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results showing below-chance decoding in controls.

claim: In Study 2, effects showed a similar pattern to Study 1.
source_text: Interestingly, effects showed a similar pattern in both studies.
evidence_reasoning: This is a comparison of the patterns observed across the two studies.

claim: In Study 2, averaged over time, no significant difference in decoding accuracy was observed between participants with and without tinnitus.
source_text: Results showed that, averaged over time, no significant difference between the participants with and without tinnitus was observed using an independent sample t-tests (t260 = 0.795, 95% CI [–0.0024, 0.0056], p = 0.428).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the t-test comparing groups.

claim: In Study 2, an equivalence test yielded a significant result indicating equivalence between the two groups.
source_text: As absence of evidence does not equal evidence of absence of an effect, we included an additional equivalence test (Walker and Nowacki, 2011). This yielded a significant result of t73.93 = −19.08, p < 0.001, indicating equivalence between the two groups
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the equivalence test.

claim: In Study 2, the group difference in prediction scores can be attributed to an altered anticipatory processing of tones presented at different levels of regularity.
source_text: Therefore, the group difference reported above can indeed be attributed to an altered (anticipatory) processing of tones presented at different levels of regularity.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the finding that basic decoding did not differ between groups.

claim: In Study 2, no significant relation was found between tinnitus distress and decoding accuracy.
source_text: Thus, building on our previous study, Spearman's rank correlation revealed no significant relation between tinnitus distress and decoding accuracy with r(30) = 0.25, p = 0.168
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claim: Tinnitus distress values did not differ significantly between Studies 1 and 2.
source_text: We additionally compared tinnitus distress values assessed by the mini-TQ (Goebel and Hiller, 1992) between Studies 1 and 2 to detect potential differences between the samples, however, results of the Welch's t-test were not significant with t(30.7) = 1.27, p = 0.214.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the comparison between studies.

claim: Group differences in predictive processing appeared to be less pronounced in Study 2 compared to Study 1.
source_text: However, group differences appeared to be less pronounced in Study 2.
evidence_reasoning: This is a comparative observation between the two studies.

claim: Bayes factors demonstrated relevant effects in both datasets in the pre-stimulus interval at around –400 ms, but values were much higher in Study 1 compared to Study 2.
source_text: Bayes factors demonstrated relevant effects in both datasets in the pre-stimulus interval at around –400 ms, however, values are much higher in Study 1 as compared to Study 2 (maximum BF 120.7 vs 7.4).
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative comparison of Bayes factors between the two studies.

claim: In Study 2, the post-stimulus interval did not reach a Bayes factor over at least 3, indicating no difference between the tinnitus and control group.
source_text: In the post-stimulus interval, the second dataset does not reach a Bayes factor over at least 3, indicating no difference between the tinnitus and control group.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the Bayes factor analysis.

claim: The choice of frequencies in Study 2 likely leads to an underestimation of the true group differences.
source_text: Overall, the choice of frequencies in Study 2 likely leads to an underestimation of the true group differences.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the impact of design choices on effect size.

claim: Bayes factors greater than 3 were solely found for subsets with higher numbers of trials (i.e. 3600 or 1500 trials).
source_text: Bayes factors greater than 3 are considered supportive of a difference (Schönbrodt and Wagenmakers, 2018). These values were solely found for subsets with higher numbers of trials (i.e. 3600 or 1500 trials).
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from the analysis of trial number effects on Bayes factors.

claim: The number of trials highly impacts the strength of effects.
source_text: Therefore, the number of trials highly impacts the strength of effects and was likely responsible for the smaller effects in Study 2 since solely 1500 trials per condition were included.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of trial number effects.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores significantly predicted whether participants experience tinnitus.
source_text: In a first model, predicting tinnitus solely by prediction scores, we could identify this as a significant predictor in Study 2 (b = 27.96, SE = 11.53, p = 0.018).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the logistic regression analysis.

claim: In Study 2, mean hearing loss did not significantly predict the presence of tinnitus.
source_text: As expected, when adding mean hearing loss to the model, it does not significantly predict the presence of tinnitus (b = 0.007, SE = 0.004, p = 0.076).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the logistic regression analysis.

claim: In Study 2, controlling for hearing loss, prediction scores still significantly predicted whether participants experience tinnitus.
source_text: Importantly (see Figure 8), controlling for the influence of hearing loss, the prediction scores still significantly predicted whether participants experience tinnitus (b = 24.63, SE = 11.51, p = 0.036).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the logistic regression analysis controlling for hearing loss.

claim: In Study 2, an increase of 1 standard deviation in the prediction score increases the odds of having tinnitus by 31%.
source_text: We included an additional odds ratio analysis, resulting in OR = 1.31, indicating an increase of 1 sd in the prediction score increases the odds of having tinnitus by 31%.
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from the odds ratio analysis.

claim: In Study 2, the presence of tinnitus significantly predicted prediction scores.
source_text: Reversing this model, we also analyzed whether the presence of tinnitus can predict prediction scores. This model was significant as well (b = 0.003, SE = 0.001, p = 0.018), indicating a statistically relevant influence of tinnitus on the prediction scores
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the reversed logistic regression analysis.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores remained a significant predictor of tinnitus even after including high-frequency hearing loss.
source_text: Prediction scores, however, remained a significant predictor of tinnitus even after including high-frequency hearing loss (b = 0.232, SE = 0.111, p = 0.040).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the logistic regression including high-frequency hearing loss.

claim: The logistic regression analysis strongly supports the notion that the main effect genuinely reflects a process related to the experience or statistical risk of experiencing tinnitus.
source_text: Overall, this analysis strongly supports the notion that the main effect genuinely reflects a process related to the experience or statistical risk of experiencing tinnitus.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the logistic regression results showing prediction scores predict tinnitus independent of hearing loss.

claim: The relevant group differences in neural representation of upcoming stimuli were successfully replicated in Study 2.
source_text: The relevant group differences were successfully replicated and cannot be explained by general tone processing, hearing loss, or tinnitus distress
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary statement about the successful replication of the main finding.

claim: The group differences in neural predictions cannot be explained by general tone processing.
source_text: The relevant group differences were successfully replicated and cannot be explained by general tone processing, hearing loss, or tinnitus distress
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the finding that basic decoding did not differ between groups.

claim: The group differences in neural predictions cannot be explained by hearing loss.
source_text: The relevant group differences were successfully replicated and cannot be explained by general tone processing, hearing loss, or tinnitus distress
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the logistic regression analysis and the matched design of Study 2.

claim: The group differences in neural predictions cannot be explained by tinnitus distress.
source_text: The relevant group differences were successfully replicated and cannot be explained by general tone processing, hearing loss, or tinnitus distress
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between prediction scores and tinnitus distress.

claim: Relatively enhanced prediction scores in the tinnitus group were shown in both studies.
source_text: Overall, relatively enhanced prediction scores in the tinnitus group were shown in both studies
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the main finding across both studies.

claim: The group differences in pre-activation patterns stem from below chance decoding for the control group.
source_text: However, it is clear that the group differences seen in both studies with respect to pre-activation patterns stems from below chance decoding for the control group, that is, a significant deactivation of anticipated carrier-frequency-specific neural patterns at late training time intervals.
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of the pattern of results showing below-chance decoding in controls.

claim: For early training time intervals, patterns between both groups are highly similar, generally marked by enhanced pre-activation of anticipated tone frequencies.
source_text: Note that for the early training time intervals (<300 ms) patterns between both groups are highly similar, generally marked by enhanced pre-activation of anticipated tone frequencies
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from the time-resolved analysis.

claim: The pre-stimulus group effect was identified at late training time intervals in both studies.
source_text: For both studies the pre-stimulus group effect was identified at late training time intervals.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the timing of the observed effects across both studies.

claim: Late training time intervals refer to patterns that are visible as small late peaks following the onset of the subsequent tone.
source_text: These refer to patterns, trained on the random sound sequences, which are visible as small late peaks (see Figures 2 and 6C). As they follow the onset of the subsequent tone, in the random tone sequence they are indicative of a reactivation of carrier-frequency-specific information
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of what the late training time intervals represent.

claim: Late training time intervals are indicative of neural processes involved in forming associations between events and formation of auditory memories.
source_text: and potentially neural processes involved in forming associations between events and hence formation of auditory memories.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the cognitive processes underlying the observed neural patterns.

claim: Below chance decoding indicates a meaningfully lacking activation of the target carrier frequency in non-tinnitus individuals for putatively higher-order auditory processes.
source_text: Applied to ordered sequences, below chance decoding indicates a meaningfully lacking activation of the target carrier frequency in non-tinnitus individuals for these putatively higher-order auditory processes.
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of what below-chance decoding represents in the context of ordered sequences.

claim: Individuals with tinnitus downregulate higher-level auditory processes once the regularity of the sound sequence is learned.
source_text: Since pre-activation of early training time windows are similar in both groups, we speculate that once the regularity of the sound sequence is learned, individuals with tinnitus downregulate these higher-level auditory processes.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed pattern of results.

claim: Individuals without tinnitus use associative contextual information to continuously 'monitor' internal models.
source_text: Translated into more conceptual terms, this could mean that individuals without tinnitus use associative contextual information to continuously 'monitor' internal models
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the cognitive processes in controls.

claim: In tinnitus, associative processes are less engaged once an internal model has formed.
source_text: and these associative processes are less engaged in tinnitus once an internal model has formed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the cognitive processes in tinnitus.

claim: In tinnitus, sensitivity to predictable stimuli could be enhanced.
source_text: Another possible explanation compatible with our effects is that, in line with predictive processes, predictions of neural representations of stimuli are pre-deactivated to minimize responses to expected stimuli. In tinnitus, this sensitivity to predictable stimuli could therefore be enhanced.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed effects.

claim: People with a tinnitus predisposition are less likely to suppress signals on account of their predictability.
source_text: People with a tinnitus predisposition are less likely to suppress that signal on account of its predictabilities
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation about signal suppression in tinnitus.

claim: Downregulations of higher-level auditory processes for predicted stimuli can indicate that auditory predictions become more strongly represented in tinnitus.
source_text: Downregulations of higher-level auditory processes for predicted stimuli can then indicate that auditory predictions become more strongly represented, and therefore harder to change through competing sensory evidence.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the observed neural patterns.

claim: Fundamental differences in auditory processing 'styles' could be a conceptual bridge to addressing why tinnitus becomes chronic and therapy resistant in some individuals.
source_text: These fundamental differences in auditory processing 'styles' could also be an interesting conceptual bridge to addressing why tinnitus becomes chronic and so therapy resistant in some individuals.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative suggestion about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: The control for hearing loss in Study 2 is unlikely to have led to a decrease in the magnitude of the effect.
source_text: An obvious assumption could be that the control for hearing loss led to a decrease in the magnitude of the effect. Even though this possibility cannot be completely excluded, we deem it very unlikely as hearing loss was neither associated with the prediction score in Study 1 (audiometry was available for the tinnitus group) nor in Study 2 assessed in the logistic regression analysis.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference based on the lack of association between hearing loss and prediction scores.

claim: The narrower frequency range in Study 2 made it more challenging for the classifier to decode tone frequencies.
source_text: However, closer frequencies lead to more similar neural patterns hence making it more challenging for a classifier to decode tone frequencies.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the impact of frequency spacing on decoding difficulty.

claim: Less reliable decoding in Study 2 likely obscured group differences to some extent.
source_text: As these classifiers were also applied to the pre-stimulus periods of the ordered sequence, less reliable decoding likely obscured group differences to some extent.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about how decoding reliability affects the ability to detect group differences.

claim: Future studies using the tone regularity paradigm should opt for a broad frequency spacing (>2 octaves).
source_text: Further to controlling for basic variables (age, sex, and hearing loss), future studies using our paradigm and analysis approach should opt for a broad frequency spacing (>2 octaves)
evidence_reasoning: This is a recommendation based on the observed impact of frequency spacing on effect size.

claim: Future studies using the tone regularity paradigm should ideally include more than 2000 trials per carrier frequency in the random sequence.
source_text: and ideally more than 2000 trials per carrier frequency in the random sequence.
evidence_reasoning: This is a recommendation based on the analysis of trial number effects on Bayes factors.

claim: The present work poses a rare instance of a replicable effect in the human neuroscientific tinnitus literature.
source_text: The present work poses the rare instance of a replicable effect in the human neuroscientific tinnitus literature, particularly of the core effect of an enhanced prediction score in tinnitus.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary statement about the significance of the replication.

claim: Study 2 excludes hearing loss as a confounding explanation for the observed differences in anticipatory neural information in tinnitus.
source_text: The results of Study 2 bear particular relevance by excluding hearing loss as a confounding explanation for the observed differences in anticipatory neural information in tinnitus.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the matched design and logistic regression results of Study 2.

claim: The robustness of the effect despite changes of some design details is worth emphasizing.
source_text: Bolstered by the recommendation as a registered report, the robustness of the effect despite changes of some design details is worth emphasizing.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about the robustness of the findings across different study designs.

claim: The narrower frequency range in Study 2 showed that the effects are to some extent generalizable and not bound to higher frequencies falling into a tinnitus-frequency range.
source_text: For example, the narrower frequency range in the pre-registered second study showed that the effects are to some extent generalizable and not bound to for example, higher-frequency falling into a tinnitus-frequency range.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the generalizability of the findings based on the replication with different frequencies.

claim: The core pre-stimulus predictive processing effect is caused by below-chance decoding accuracy in the non-tinnitus group.
source_text: We concluded that the core pre-stimulus predictive processing effect is caused by a below-chance decoding accuracy in the non-tinnitus group.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results showing below-chance decoding in controls.

claim: The original notion of a more generally enhanced prediction score in tinnitus individuals is likely too simplistic.
source_text: This indicates that our original notion of a more generally enhanced prediction score in tinnitus individuals is likely too simplistic.
evidence_reasoning: This is a revision of the initial interpretation based on the detailed analysis of the results.

claim: Both studies equivalently reveal a group difference in neural representation of upcoming stimuli before their onset.
source_text: Despite some changes in the details of the paradigm, both studies equivalently reveal a group difference in neural representation, based on multivariate pattern analysis, of upcoming stimuli before their onset.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary statement from the abstract about the main finding across both studies.

claim: Individuals with tinnitus engage anticipatory auditory predictions differently to controls.
source_text: These data strongly suggest that individuals with tinnitus engage anticipatory auditory predictions differently to controls.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the observed group differences in pre-stimulus neural patterns.

claim: The observation of different predictive processes is robust and replicable.
source_text: While the observation of different predictive processes is robust and replicable
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary statement about the robustness of the main finding.

claim: The precise neurocognitive mechanism underlying the different predictive processes calls for further, ideally longitudinal, studies.
source_text: the precise neurocognitive mechanism underlying it calls for further, ideally longitudinal, studies to establish its role as a potential contributor to, and/or consequence of, tinnitus.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about the need for future research to understand the mechanisms.
